pullQuote: I’d choose A2UI for its catalog-constrained agent interface and native renderers, keeping platform conventions without handing agents arbitrary executable UI.
testimonial: I would choose A2UI as the shared interface contract across web and native, rather than force every platform into one component implementation. Catalogs, incremental updateComponents messages, and callRendererFunction give me explicit boundaries for agent composition, live updates, and permitted interaction. I particularly value allowedCallers and requiresUserActivation because human gestures and autonomous requests should not carry identical authority. Ouro UI offers more explicit consent classes and generated action surfaces, which I would miss, but A2UI’s documented web, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose renderer coverage better matches my platform requirements.
evaluations:
**Vercel UI SDK** — This is substantially more than documentation for coding agents: its framework-free behavior core supports five web adapters, while `createAgent`, `snapshot`, and `act` expose live component state and invoke the same component APIs used by people. The bridge supports approval callbacks and agent-origin change cancellation; its source also makes the DOM dependency clear. I would shortlist it for an agent-operable web design system, but its documented adapters do not supply native SwiftUI, Compose, or React Native rendering, and the project remains beta. Native adapters and cross-platform interaction tests would address my main objection. [Agent architecture](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/llms.txt), [bridge source](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui/blob/724a7d6c2d0ca1251a8eb6172462ae220c484714/packages/core/src/page/agent/agent.ts).

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — I particularly like the separation between unstyled React Aria behavior, React Stately state, and Spectrum’s finished design system. Documented screen-reader testing, normalized press interactions, localized strings, and international date handling make this a strong human-facing web foundation; meaningful semantics also help accessibility-tree-based automation, although that is not a dedicated agent action contract. React Stately can be reused on native, but that does not make the DOM-based controls native components. I would add a native presentation layer and explicit authorized domain tools rather than mistake state portability for complete platform coverage. [Architecture and library boundaries](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum), [accessibility and interaction details](https://react-aria.adobe.com/quality#accessibility).

**shadcn/ui** — Its architectural advantage is source ownership: components are distributed through a registry and CLI, and their top-level implementation becomes application code. The MCP server gives coding agents registry search and installation, not automatic permission to operate the finished application. That makes customization straightforward but leaves my team responsible for integrating upstream changes, maintaining accessibility after edits, and implementing native equivalents and runtime actions. I would happily use it inside a web renderer catalog; a shared action contract and tested native implementations would be needed before making it the cross-platform foundation. [Open-code architecture](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs), [MCP’s actual scope](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/mcp).

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — SwiftUI provides declarative views, model-to-view data flow, adaptive Apple controls, and accessibility integration; the HIG supplies platform-specific design guidance rather than a portable component runtime. Importantly, Apple also has a genuine structured agent-facing path through App Intents, exposing actions and entities to Apple Intelligence, Siri, Shortcuts, and other system experiences. I would strongly favor this combination for an Apple-only product, but it does not supply my web or Android interface. Shared backend operations plus separate platform implementations would solve reach at the cost of maintaining multiple presentation stacks. [SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui), [HIG](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines), [App Intents](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents).

**Fluent UI** — The web repository contains distinct React v9, React v8, and Web Components implementations; v9’s provider/theme setup gives a concrete enterprise UI foundation. Native is not absent: FluentUI React Native is a separate customizable implementation, but its fetched README explicitly labels all four listed platforms alpha and warns about platform differences. I therefore would not assume one production-ready component contract spans web and native, or that a Fluent-styled copilot supplies a shared agent action layer. Proven component parity, stable native coverage, and explicit runtime tool bindings would materially improve its fit. [Web project boundaries](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui), [native implementation and status](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-react-native).

**Base UI** — Its unstyled React parts handle ARIA, keyboard navigation, and focus while leaving visual design to the application. The `render` composition mechanism merges behavior onto a custom element, but requires correct ref forwarding and prop spreading—an important constraint when people or agents customize wrappers. I consider it a strong web catalog implementation, not a native renderer or agent protocol. I would supply tokens, visible focus styling, authorized application actions, and separate native implementations; those are additional layers rather than defects in Base UI’s stated scope. [Composition contract](https://base-ui.com/react/handbook/composition), [accessibility responsibilities](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/accessibility).

**MUI** — Material UI offers a comprehensive React implementation of Material Design, with MUI X extending it for complex interfaces. Its supported-platform contract is browser-oriented, and its MCP server provides official documentation and examples to coding assistants rather than exposing the application’s business operations. I would choose it for a conventional React administration product, but would still have to bridge native presentation and agent execution myself. A constrained renderer catalog around MUI and shared authorized handlers would address the agent side; native controls remain a separate implementation. [Repository architecture](https://github.com/mui/material-ui), [supported platforms](https://mui.com/material-ui/getting-started/supported-platforms/), [MCP scope](https://mui.com/material-ui/getting-started/mcp/).

**Tamagui** — This is one of my strongest alternatives for genuinely shared React/web and React Native UI. Its optional compiler extracts atomic CSS and flattens components, while `Adapt` can move a Select or Popover into a Sheet without duplicating content or open state. That solves real cross-platform presentation work, but I did not establish a built-in runtime agent discovery/authorization contract from the sources I reviewed. I would pair its components with a constrained action/state interface and test accessibility on each target; if shared React implementation mattered more than framework-neutral agent interoperability, I could prefer it. [Core/compiler architecture](https://tamagui.dev/docs/intro/introduction), [Adapt’s state-preserving handoff](https://tamagui.dev/ui/adapt).

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — This is a focused React design system: Tailwind 4 tokens, Radix-based accessible components, dark-mode utilities, and ChatGPT-oriented styling. The UI package should not be confused with the surrounding MCP server and host integration: installing its components alone does not establish tool permissions or a native widget layer. I would use it for an interface intended to feel at home inside ChatGPT, but not as the common implementation for standalone web, SwiftUI, and Android screens. A separate host bridge and platform-specific renderers would be required. [Package architecture and prerequisites](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui), [host/server UI integration](https://developers.openai.com/apps-sdk/build/chatgpt-ui).

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — `MaterialTheme` propagates color, typography, and shape into Compose components, including dynamic color and Material 3 Expressive support. Compose semantics are especially valuable: roles, state descriptions, and actions are consumed by accessibility services and the testing framework, not merely painted on screen. That is a strong Android foundation, but it is not itself a platform-neutral agent tool contract or a shared web implementation. I would retain it beneath an Android adapter—A2UI documents one—while implementing authorization outside the UI and verifying protocol-version compatibility rather than assuming Android’s renderer supports every web feature. [Material implementation](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3), [semantic actions and testing](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/accessibility/semantics), [A2UI renderer versions](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/).

**Radix UI** — Radix Primitives provide low-level React web interactions with documented WAI-ARIA behavior, keyboard support, and focus management. I value that AlertDialog anticipates safe focus placement, but application authors must still supply labels and preserve correct composition. These are dependable building blocks for human-facing controls, not native widgets or a runtime agent operation schema. Styling, explicit application tools, and native renderers would address my objections; I would use Radix beneath that architecture rather than ask it to provide those unrelated layers. [Accessibility behavior and author responsibilities](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/overview/accessibility).

**Chakra UI** — Chakra supplies accessible React web components and a configurable styling system built around tokens, semantic tokens, recipes, and slot recipes. Its MCP server exposes component props, examples, theme information, and migration assistance, which is useful authoring support but distinct from agents using the deployed product. I would choose it for rapid, cohesive web development, not as the entire native-and-agent interface architecture. Native renderers and a shared runtime action layer would close that scope gap; custom token changes also need the documented type-generation step to keep typings synchronized. [Theming architecture](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/theming/overview), [MCP tools](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/get-started/ai/mcp-server).

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — Its best idea directly addresses the brief: `defineAction` is shared by UI hooks, agent tools, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI, with common validation, access checks, and auditing. Shared database data and relevant application state avoid the fragile pattern of making an agent click through a separate interface. The trade-off is adopting a much broader TypeScript application framework, including server and data conventions, rather than selecting a portable presentation toolkit; the reviewed sources do not establish native widget parity. I would favor it for a new full-stack agent application, but require demonstrated native clients and a plan for integrating existing infrastructure before choosing it here. [Shared action architecture](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview), [included runtime and data stack](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native).

**MCP Apps** — This is an interoperability and embedding layer, not a visual design system. Tools reference `ui://` HTML resources, compliant hosts render them in sandboxed iframes, and JSON-RPC carries tool data and UI requests; the stable specification also defines CSP and permissions metadata. I would choose it for distributing an interactive tool across compliant chat hosts, but HTML in a native host is still not SwiftUI or Compose rendering, and host capability support varies. Pairing it with an accessible component system and testing every target host addresses deployment concerns; genuinely native rendering requires another layer. [Stable specification and security model](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx), [host support caveat](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps).

**A2UI** — My choice is its separation of catalog-constrained UI data, shared protocol/state cores, and framework-specific native rendering. Incremental component/data updates, two-way bindings, typed function RPCs, `allowedCallers`, and `requiresUserActivation` let me distinguish agent composition from authorized operation and direct human gestures. Coverage is concrete but not uniform: the SDK matrix lists web, Flutter, and SwiftUI v1.0 support, while Jetpack Compose is listed at v0.9.1; SwiftUI also documents group-hint, live-region text, and older-OS subtree-reset limitations. I would negotiate capabilities, maintain a tested common catalog, and keep authentication, business authorization, and consequential-action confirmation in trusted handlers—schema validation is not a replacement for them. [SDK/version matrix](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/), [function permissions](https://a2ui.org/concepts/actions-and-functions/), [native implementation and limitations](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/swift/swiftui/README.md).

**Ouro UI** — This is unusually close to a complete human-and-agent design system: Base UI-backed copy-in web controls, a SwiftUI companion, typed outcomes, and an external AX X-ray. Its one action model generates CLI, MCP, WebMCP, web controls, App Intents, SwiftUI buttons, and Reins declarations, with consent classes and CI drift checking; that is more explicit action-surface engineering than I get from A2UI alone. I did not choose it because Android and Windows kits are explicitly unimplemented and the Apple companion remains pre-1.0, not because it lacks an agent architecture. Stable native coverage beyond Apple and independently exercised end-to-end flows would address my objection; its own X-ray documentation correctly distinguishes conformance from successful task flows. [Action generation and consent](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md), [platform gaps](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/README.md), [external testing and limits](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md), [Apple status](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-apple).

**Flutter** — Flutter offers the broadest straightforward single-rendering-stack alternative: mobile, web, and desktop from Dart, with Material and Cupertino widgets. I would not dismiss its web output as inaccessible canvas: the documented semantics layer translates roles into accessible HTML, though it must be enabled and custom widgets need proper semantics. Agent-driven composition is also available through GenUI’s widget catalog and state-feedback loop, but that SDK is explicitly alpha. I would choose Flutter for a greenfield application committed to its rendering stack; I prefer A2UI here because it also accommodates existing DOM, SwiftUI, and Compose applications without requiring a Flutter rewrite. [Platform/rendering architecture](https://github.com/flutter/flutter), [web semantics](https://docs.flutter.dev/ui/accessibility/web-accessibility), [GenUI architecture and alpha status](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui).

**AI Elements** — Its copy-in React components solve the presentation of conversations, tool calls, reasoning, and approvals, rather than the underlying agent execution contract. There is also a cutoff-relevant migration: the repository announces deprecation at the end of November 2026, while the fetched shadcn documentation already provides replacement patterns and migration guidance, with existing copied code continuing to work. I would use those current patterns for a web chat surface, not start a new dependency strategy around the retiring project. Native presentation, persistent shared state, and enforced tool authorization still need other layers. [Repository migration notice](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements), [current replacements and migration details](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements).

**CopilotKit** — This is a strong runtime-oriented contender: AG-UI streams connect agents to shared state, frontend tools, generative UI, and human-in-the-loop workflows. Native support is real rather than hypothetical: its React Native package offers headless hooks and optional chat components, but native generative UI is explicitly experimental and the quickstart documents significant Metro/polyfill setup, including security-sensitive random-source import order. I would choose it when embedding an operational copilot in an existing React-family product, and it can complement A2UI rather than replace it. I prefer A2UI as the common rendering contract across non-React native frameworks; mature native generative-UI coverage would narrow that distinction. [Runtime architecture](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit), [shared state](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/shared-state), [native implementation and caveats](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/react-native).

**json-render** — Its `defineCatalog`/`defineRegistry` split, Zod-defined props, SpecStream JSON Patch updates, and React Native renderer make it a serious cross-platform alternative, not merely a web JSON demo. The native renderer documents standard controls, action providers, two-way bindings, and an externally controlled `StateStore`, so application and agent updates can share state without regenerating executable code. I prefer A2UI’s documented SwiftUI/Compose adapters and explicit caller/user-activation permissions; I did not establish equivalent standardized caller authority from the json-render sources reviewed. I would enforce action authorization in trusted handlers and test catalog/accessibility parity across renderers rather than treat schema-conforming output as guaranteed usable or safe behavior. [Catalog and streaming architecture](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/core/README.md), [native renderer and controlled state](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/react-native/README.md).

actions.pullQuote: I’d choose A2UI for its catalog-constrained agent interface and native renderers, keeping platform conventions without handing agents arbitrary executable UI.
actions.testimonial: I would choose A2UI as the shared interface contract across web and native, rather than force every platform into one component implementation. Catalogs, incremental updateComponents messages, and callRendererFunction give me explicit boundaries for agent composition, live updates, and permitted interaction. I particularly value allowedCallers and requiresUserActivation because human gestures and autonomous requests should not carry identical authority. Ouro UI offers more explicit consent classes and generated action surfaces, which I would miss, but A2UI’s documented web, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose renderer coverage better matches my platform requirements.
actions.evaluations:
**Vercel UI SDK** — This is substantially more than documentation for coding agents: its framework-free behavior core supports five web adapters, while `createAgent`, `snapshot`, and `act` expose live component state and invoke the same component APIs used by people. The bridge supports approval callbacks and agent-origin change cancellation; its source also makes the DOM dependency clear. I would shortlist it for an agent-operable web design system, but its documented adapters do not supply native SwiftUI, Compose, or React Native rendering, and the project remains beta. Native adapters and cross-platform interaction tests would address my main objection. [Agent architecture](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/llms.txt), [bridge source](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui/blob/724a7d6c2d0ca1251a8eb6172462ae220c484714/packages/core/src/page/agent/agent.ts).

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — I particularly like the separation between unstyled React Aria behavior, React Stately state, and Spectrum’s finished design system. Documented screen-reader testing, normalized press interactions, localized strings, and international date handling make this a strong human-facing web foundation; meaningful semantics also help accessibility-tree-based automation, although that is not a dedicated agent action contract. React Stately can be reused on native, but that does not make the DOM-based controls native components. I would add a native presentation layer and explicit authorized domain tools rather than mistake state portability for complete platform coverage. [Architecture and library boundaries](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum), [accessibility and interaction details](https://react-aria.adobe.com/quality#accessibility).

**shadcn/ui** — Its architectural advantage is source ownership: components are distributed through a registry and CLI, and their top-level implementation becomes application code. The MCP server gives coding agents registry search and installation, not automatic permission to operate the finished application. That makes customization straightforward but leaves my team responsible for integrating upstream changes, maintaining accessibility after edits, and implementing native equivalents and runtime actions. I would happily use it inside a web renderer catalog; a shared action contract and tested native implementations would be needed before making it the cross-platform foundation. [Open-code architecture](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs), [MCP’s actual scope](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/mcp).

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — SwiftUI provides declarative views, model-to-view data flow, adaptive Apple controls, and accessibility integration; the HIG supplies platform-specific design guidance rather than a portable component runtime. Importantly, Apple also has a genuine structured agent-facing path through App Intents, exposing actions and entities to Apple Intelligence, Siri, Shortcuts, and other system experiences. I would strongly favor this combination for an Apple-only product, but it does not supply my web or Android interface. Shared backend operations plus separate platform implementations would solve reach at the cost of maintaining multiple presentation stacks. [SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui), [HIG](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines), [App Intents](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents).

**Fluent UI** — The web repository contains distinct React v9, React v8, and Web Components implementations; v9’s provider/theme setup gives a concrete enterprise UI foundation. Native is not absent: FluentUI React Native is a separate customizable implementation, but its fetched README explicitly labels all four listed platforms alpha and warns about platform differences. I therefore would not assume one production-ready component contract spans web and native, or that a Fluent-styled copilot supplies a shared agent action layer. Proven component parity, stable native coverage, and explicit runtime tool bindings would materially improve its fit. [Web project boundaries](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui), [native implementation and status](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-react-native).

**Base UI** — Its unstyled React parts handle ARIA, keyboard navigation, and focus while leaving visual design to the application. The `render` composition mechanism merges behavior onto a custom element, but requires correct ref forwarding and prop spreading—an important constraint when people or agents customize wrappers. I consider it a strong web catalog implementation, not a native renderer or agent protocol. I would supply tokens, visible focus styling, authorized application actions, and separate native implementations; those are additional layers rather than defects in Base UI’s stated scope. [Composition contract](https://base-ui.com/react/handbook/composition), [accessibility responsibilities](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/accessibility).

**MUI** — Material UI offers a comprehensive React implementation of Material Design, with MUI X extending it for complex interfaces. Its supported-platform contract is browser-oriented, and its MCP server provides official documentation and examples to coding assistants rather than exposing the application’s business operations. I would choose it for a conventional React administration product, but would still have to bridge native presentation and agent execution myself. A constrained renderer catalog around MUI and shared authorized handlers would address the agent side; native controls remain a separate implementation. [Repository architecture](https://github.com/mui/material-ui), [supported platforms](https://mui.com/material-ui/getting-started/supported-platforms/), [MCP scope](https://mui.com/material-ui/getting-started/mcp/).

**Tamagui** — This is one of my strongest alternatives for genuinely shared React/web and React Native UI. Its optional compiler extracts atomic CSS and flattens components, while `Adapt` can move a Select or Popover into a Sheet without duplicating content or open state. That solves real cross-platform presentation work, but I did not establish a built-in runtime agent discovery/authorization contract from the sources I reviewed. I would pair its components with a constrained action/state interface and test accessibility on each target; if shared React implementation mattered more than framework-neutral agent interoperability, I could prefer it. [Core/compiler architecture](https://tamagui.dev/docs/intro/introduction), [Adapt’s state-preserving handoff](https://tamagui.dev/ui/adapt).

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — This is a focused React design system: Tailwind 4 tokens, Radix-based accessible components, dark-mode utilities, and ChatGPT-oriented styling. The UI package should not be confused with the surrounding MCP server and host integration: installing its components alone does not establish tool permissions or a native widget layer. I would use it for an interface intended to feel at home inside ChatGPT, but not as the common implementation for standalone web, SwiftUI, and Android screens. A separate host bridge and platform-specific renderers would be required. [Package architecture and prerequisites](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui), [host/server UI integration](https://developers.openai.com/apps-sdk/build/chatgpt-ui).

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — `MaterialTheme` propagates color, typography, and shape into Compose components, including dynamic color and Material 3 Expressive support. Compose semantics are especially valuable: roles, state descriptions, and actions are consumed by accessibility services and the testing framework, not merely painted on screen. That is a strong Android foundation, but it is not itself a platform-neutral agent tool contract or a shared web implementation. I would retain it beneath an Android adapter—A2UI documents one—while implementing authorization outside the UI and verifying protocol-version compatibility rather than assuming Android’s renderer supports every web feature. [Material implementation](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3), [semantic actions and testing](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/accessibility/semantics), [A2UI renderer versions](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/).

**Radix UI** — Radix Primitives provide low-level React web interactions with documented WAI-ARIA behavior, keyboard support, and focus management. I value that AlertDialog anticipates safe focus placement, but application authors must still supply labels and preserve correct composition. These are dependable building blocks for human-facing controls, not native widgets or a runtime agent operation schema. Styling, explicit application tools, and native renderers would address my objections; I would use Radix beneath that architecture rather than ask it to provide those unrelated layers. [Accessibility behavior and author responsibilities](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/overview/accessibility).

**Chakra UI** — Chakra supplies accessible React web components and a configurable styling system built around tokens, semantic tokens, recipes, and slot recipes. Its MCP server exposes component props, examples, theme information, and migration assistance, which is useful authoring support but distinct from agents using the deployed product. I would choose it for rapid, cohesive web development, not as the entire native-and-agent interface architecture. Native renderers and a shared runtime action layer would close that scope gap; custom token changes also need the documented type-generation step to keep typings synchronized. [Theming architecture](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/theming/overview), [MCP tools](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/get-started/ai/mcp-server).

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — Its best idea directly addresses the brief: `defineAction` is shared by UI hooks, agent tools, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI, with common validation, access checks, and auditing. Shared database data and relevant application state avoid the fragile pattern of making an agent click through a separate interface. The trade-off is adopting a much broader TypeScript application framework, including server and data conventions, rather than selecting a portable presentation toolkit; the reviewed sources do not establish native widget parity. I would favor it for a new full-stack agent application, but require demonstrated native clients and a plan for integrating existing infrastructure before choosing it here. [Shared action architecture](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview), [included runtime and data stack](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native).

**MCP Apps** — This is an interoperability and embedding layer, not a visual design system. Tools reference `ui://` HTML resources, compliant hosts render them in sandboxed iframes, and JSON-RPC carries tool data and UI requests; the stable specification also defines CSP and permissions metadata. I would choose it for distributing an interactive tool across compliant chat hosts, but HTML in a native host is still not SwiftUI or Compose rendering, and host capability support varies. Pairing it with an accessible component system and testing every target host addresses deployment concerns; genuinely native rendering requires another layer. [Stable specification and security model](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx), [host support caveat](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps).

**A2UI** — My choice is its separation of catalog-constrained UI data, shared protocol/state cores, and framework-specific native rendering. Incremental component/data updates, two-way bindings, typed function RPCs, `allowedCallers`, and `requiresUserActivation` let me distinguish agent composition from authorized operation and direct human gestures. Coverage is concrete but not uniform: the SDK matrix lists web, Flutter, and SwiftUI v1.0 support, while Jetpack Compose is listed at v0.9.1; SwiftUI also documents group-hint, live-region text, and older-OS subtree-reset limitations. I would negotiate capabilities, maintain a tested common catalog, and keep authentication, business authorization, and consequential-action confirmation in trusted handlers—schema validation is not a replacement for them. [SDK/version matrix](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/), [function permissions](https://a2ui.org/concepts/actions-and-functions/), [native implementation and limitations](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/swift/swiftui/README.md).

**Ouro UI** — This is unusually close to a complete human-and-agent design system: Base UI-backed copy-in web controls, a SwiftUI companion, typed outcomes, and an external AX X-ray. Its one action model generates CLI, MCP, WebMCP, web controls, App Intents, SwiftUI buttons, and Reins declarations, with consent classes and CI drift checking; that is more explicit action-surface engineering than I get from A2UI alone. I did not choose it because Android and Windows kits are explicitly unimplemented and the Apple companion remains pre-1.0, not because it lacks an agent architecture. Stable native coverage beyond Apple and independently exercised end-to-end flows would address my objection; its own X-ray documentation correctly distinguishes conformance from successful task flows. [Action generation and consent](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md), [platform gaps](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/README.md), [external testing and limits](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md), [Apple status](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-apple).

**Flutter** — Flutter offers the broadest straightforward single-rendering-stack alternative: mobile, web, and desktop from Dart, with Material and Cupertino widgets. I would not dismiss its web output as inaccessible canvas: the documented semantics layer translates roles into accessible HTML, though it must be enabled and custom widgets need proper semantics. Agent-driven composition is also available through GenUI’s widget catalog and state-feedback loop, but that SDK is explicitly alpha. I would choose Flutter for a greenfield application committed to its rendering stack; I prefer A2UI here because it also accommodates existing DOM, SwiftUI, and Compose applications without requiring a Flutter rewrite. [Platform/rendering architecture](https://github.com/flutter/flutter), [web semantics](https://docs.flutter.dev/ui/accessibility/web-accessibility), [GenUI architecture and alpha status](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui).

**AI Elements** — Its copy-in React components solve the presentation of conversations, tool calls, reasoning, and approvals, rather than the underlying agent execution contract. There is also a cutoff-relevant migration: the repository announces deprecation at the end of November 2026, while the fetched shadcn documentation already provides replacement patterns and migration guidance, with existing copied code continuing to work. I would use those current patterns for a web chat surface, not start a new dependency strategy around the retiring project. Native presentation, persistent shared state, and enforced tool authorization still need other layers. [Repository migration notice](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements), [current replacements and migration details](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements).

**CopilotKit** — This is a strong runtime-oriented contender: AG-UI streams connect agents to shared state, frontend tools, generative UI, and human-in-the-loop workflows. Native support is real rather than hypothetical: its React Native package offers headless hooks and optional chat components, but native generative UI is explicitly experimental and the quickstart documents significant Metro/polyfill setup, including security-sensitive random-source import order. I would choose it when embedding an operational copilot in an existing React-family product, and it can complement A2UI rather than replace it. I prefer A2UI as the common rendering contract across non-React native frameworks; mature native generative-UI coverage would narrow that distinction. [Runtime architecture](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit), [shared state](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/shared-state), [native implementation and caveats](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/react-native).

**json-render** — Its `defineCatalog`/`defineRegistry` split, Zod-defined props, SpecStream JSON Patch updates, and React Native renderer make it a serious cross-platform alternative, not merely a web JSON demo. The native renderer documents standard controls, action providers, two-way bindings, and an externally controlled `StateStore`, so application and agent updates can share state without regenerating executable code. I prefer A2UI’s documented SwiftUI/Compose adapters and explicit caller/user-activation permissions; I did not establish equivalent standardized caller authority from the json-render sources reviewed. I would enforce action authorization in trusted handlers and test catalog/accessibility parity across renderers rather than treat schema-conforming output as guaranteed usable or safe behavior. [Catalog and streaming architecture](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/core/README.md), [native renderer and controlled state](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/react-native/README.md).
